messages.subject: Re: parboot() and parallel processing
messages.subject_clean: parboot() and parallel processing
messages.body_plain:
Thanks so much Ken! I was able to get it all figured out using the code you provided! Worked perfectly!

On Thursday, May 16, 2019 at 9:16:37 PM UTC-4, Ken Kellner wrote:
> This error is due to the way unmarked fits updated models with new formulas or datasets, which is required for parboot() and thus mb.gof.test(). Some unmarked helper functions can't always handle situations where the original fitted model had expressions passed as arguments, as you have with
> unmarked::occu(as.formula(x[[1]]),x[[2]])
>
> You can work around this issue in an extremely hacky way by modifying the saved `call` attribute of the unmarked fit object to trick unmarked into using the right formula and dataset. I don't have your full dataset to demonstrate but here's an example with the built in frog dataset:
>
> data(frogs)
> pferUMF <- unmarkedFrameOccu(pfer.bin)
> # add some fake covariates for illustration
> siteCovs(pferUMF) <- data.frame(sitevar1 = rnorm(numSites(pferUMF)))
> # observation covariates are in site-major, observation-minor order
> obsCovs(pferUMF) <- data.frame(obsvar1 = rnorm(numSites(pferUMF) * obsNum(pferUMF)))
>
> mods <- list(
>              list(formula='~1~1',data=pferUMF),
>              list(formula='~obsvar1~1', data=pferUMF)
>              )
>
> run_um <- function(x){unmarked::occu(as.formula(x[[1]]),x[[2]])} #here is where the issue comes in
>
> cl <- makeCluster(detectCores()-1)
>
> mods_out <- parLapply(cl=cl, X=mods, run_um)
>
> #GOF
>
> #Would need to change pferUMF here to your dataset name
> clusterExport(cl, c('pferUMF', 'mods', 'mods_out'))
>
> run_gof <- function(i){
>
>   #Modify call attribute of the model to work around issue
>   new_call <- call('occu',as.formula(mods[[i]][[1]]),mods[[i]][[2]])
>
>   this_mod <- mods_out[[i]]
>   this_mod@call[2] <- new_call[2]
>   this_mod@call[3] <- new_call[3]
>
>   #Don't want to set this to parallel also, as you are
>   #already in a parallel loop
>   #note change in nsim vs your code
>   AICcmodavg::mb.gof.test(this_mod, nsim=10, plot.hist=FALSE,
>                           report=NULL, parallel=FALSE)
> }
>
> #List of GOF output in same order as mods_out
> gof_out <- parLapply(cl=cl, X=1:length(mods_out), run_gof)
>
>
> stopCluster(cl)
>
>
> However, I think you may be better off not running your GOF tests in parallel this way. If you run each GOF test in a separate core, as you are attempting to do, you can't also have mb.gof.test() run simulations in parallel (since each parallelized GOF test is, by definition, only able to use a single core). The number of simulations running in each mb.gof.test()  in your code (1000) is likely much higher than the total number of models you have. Thus to me it makes more sense to just run the GOF tests in a regular non-parallel for loop or similar, and let mb.gof.test() run in in parallel. Unfortunately you still have to correct for the problem above:
>
> gof_out <- vector("list", length=length(mods_out))
> for (i in seq_along(mods_out)){
>
>   new_call <- call('occu',as.formula(mods[[i]][[1]]),mods[[i]][[2]])
>
>   this_mod <- mods_out[[i]]
>   this_mod@call[2] <- new_call[2]
>   this_mod@call[3] <- new_call[3]
>
>   #Note change in nsim vs your code
>   gof_out[[i]] <- AICcmodavg::mb.gof.test(this_mod, nsim=10, plot.hist=FALSE,
>                                           report=NULL, parallel=TRUE)
> }
>
>
>
> On Thursday, May 16, 2019 at 4:27:27 PM UTC-4, Carly Scott wrote:
> > To whomever might be able to help!
> >
> > I am trying to use this same logic to run mb.gof.test in parallel on a remote cluster after also running my models in parallel on the cluster, however I keep getting the following error:
> >
> >      Error in checkForRemoteErrors(lapply(cl, recvResult)) :
> >   10 nodes produced errors; first error: object 'x' not found
> >
> > I don't even know what object 'x' is here!!!
> >
> > This is my code:
> >
> > bear3<-unmarkedFrameOccu(y=y3, siteCovs=site3, obsCovs=list(month=month3[,2:289]))
> >
> > run_um<-function(x) {unmarked::occu(as.formula(x[[1]]),x[[2]])}
> >
> > clusterExport(cl, c("bear3", "run_um"))
> >
> > mods<-list(bearglobdet3<-list(formula='~cat+hum+elev+topo+tree+month~1', data=bear3),
> >               bearglobabu3<-list(formula='~1~cat+hum+elev+topo+tree', data=bear3))
> >
> > modsout<-parLapply(cl=cl, X=mods, fun=run_um)
> >
> > #now to do goodness of fit
> > clusterExport(cl, "modsout")
> >
> > clusterSetRNGStream(cl, 123)
> >
> > gofout<-clusterEvalQ(cl, {
> >   library(AICcmodavg)
> >   mb.gof.test(modsout[[1]], nsim=1000, plot.hist=TRUE, report=NULL, parallel=TRUE)
> > }) # which results in the error
> >
> >  Any advice you have would be very useful for me, I am still relatively new to r so its probably a simple mistake somewhere! I have a ton of goodness of fit tests to run on my very small lab computer, which is why I am trying to make use of the remote server!
> >
> > Thanks in advance.
> >
> >
> > On Friday, August 1, 2014 at 1:43:04 PM UTC-4, MP wrote:
> > > I am able to get parboot to run in parallel instances, in my case in 8 clusters.  I was wondering if there's a way to combine each of the resulting outputs into a single parboot class object?
> > > I got as far as creating a data frame combining the SSE, Chisq, and freemanTukey estimates between the 8 parboot instances, but I'd like to have it all together in a handy package.

messages.subject: Colext- Estimating psi along elevational gradient in different years
messages.subject_clean: Colext- Estimating psi along elevational gradient in different years
messages.body_plain:
Dear unmarked users,

I`m using the colext function to understand the impact of hurricane Maria on birds and frogs distribution in Puerto Rico.

I`m working with 68 sampling sites in three transects along an elevational gradient (~75-1030meters), three primary visits (years), and 17 secondary occasions.

One of my main questions in this study is to determine if species changed their distributions along the elevational gradient among the years (especially in the year after the hurricane).

As I understand, Predict function cannot give me yearly estimates of psi. So, I`m using smoothed and projected values. Nevertheless, I would like to obtain estimates of psi along the elevation gradient for each year.
Is there a way to obtain these values in unmarked?

Thank you very much!

Best,

Marconi Campos

messages.body_plain:
Marconi,

>From my understanding (more knowledgeable folks should feel free to correct me), you need to predict initial psi and colonization (col) and extinction (ext) rates for each subsequent year, then project forward using this formula (using underscore for subscripts):

psi_t = (psi_t-1 x (1 - ext_t-1)) + (col_t-1 x (1 - psi_t-1))

In other words, psi in a year is calculated by psi in the previous year x those sites that don't go extinct (1-ext) plus the colonization rate for those sites that weren't occupied (1-psi).

I exported my prediction outputs to excel and set up stepwise calculations in a spreadsheet, but someone better at R should easily be able to do this in R with predict outputs.

You can predict with two covariates as below, depending on whether you are using year as a factor or continuous variable.

#One factor covar and one continuous covar.  Results will be predicted for each factor level when at mean continuous covar level.
NewData <- data.frame(Area=0, Observer=factor(c("AW","KE","NNC","Multiple","Other")))
Results.predict<-predict(fm, newdata=NewData,"det")
write.table(ResultsTable<-c(NewData,Results.predict))

#One factor covar and one continuous covar for psi.  Results will be predicted psi for continuous covar values for given factor level.
NewData <- data.frame(Area=seq(-0.8,5,by=0.1), Observer=factor("KE", levels=c("AW","KE","NNC","Multiple","Other")))
Results.predict<-predict(fm, "psi", newdata=NewData)
write.table(ResultsTable<-c(NewData,Results.predict))

#Two continuous covars (for interaction).  Must have same number of intervals, so use length.out instead of by interval
NewData <- data.frame(RRdist=seq(-1.2,3.2,length.out=20), ProporHab=seq(-3.3,1.1,length.out=20))
Results.predict <- predict(fm,"psi",newdata=NewData)
write.table(ResultsTable<-c(NewData,Results.predict))

#Two continuous covars (for interaction).  Mean of first covar and range of values for second
NewData <- data.frame(RRdist=0, ProporHab=seq(-3.3,1.1,by=0.1))
Results.predict <- predict(fm,"psi",newdata=NewData)
write.table(ResultsTable<-c(NewData,Results.predict))

You can also use the min and max functions to population the sequence arguments in creating a data frame to predict into:
Instead of RRdist=seq(-1.2,3.2,length.out=20) use RRdist=seq(min(umf@siteCovs$RRdist, na.rm = TRUE),max(umf@siteCovs$RRdist, na.rm = TRUE),length.out=20)

Let me know if you have follow up questions.

-Alex

Hello Alex,

Thank you very much for all the info!

I`m able to estimate psi at each year by using smoothed and projected values. No problem at that end.  But what I really want is to compare the elevation profile among the three years.

I`m using a similar approach that you describe to make predictions using several covariates ( including factor and continuous variables), and everything is working fine with this too.

nd1 <- data.frame(Elev=seq(-2.02600,1.41557,length=100),Slope.mean=0,year=factor("2019",levels=c("2015","2016","2019")),PA=factor("YES",levels=c("NO","YES")))
nd1

But again, what I want is to see is how psi along with the elevational gradient changes at different years. Let`s say that, for example, previous the hurricane the species had higher occupancy probability at intermediary elevations ( hump-shaped curve) and after the hurricane, the species had higher occupancy probabilities at the lowlands.

I have tried different approaches in the past using the single-season approach, but never with colext...

Maybe I missed something from your message. I`m going to read and digest the reference that you have sent me.

Again, thanks for your help.

Best, Marconi

messages.subject_clean: [unmarked] Re: Colext- Estimating psi along elevational gradient in different years
messages.body_plain:
Please ignore if this is stating the obvious.  To "compare the elevation profile among the three years" you'll need to construct (explicitly) the associated "elevation profile" effect using the parameters in your model.  You'll then need to estimate the precision of that effect either using the Delta Method using the estimated covariance matrix from the colext output or  using a bootstrap.  Comparing the elevation profile among the three years is certainly a legitimate objective.  It just needs to be made explicit in terms of the parameters in the model.  That's the hard part.  Estimating the precision will be the easy (or at least easier) part.  I say all of this without a specific example because I don't see where you've given the model you're using.  (I'm reluctant to guess at the model just from the data frame you've presented.)

Jim

messages.body_plain:
Thanks, that helps clarify things.  Since hurricane Maria hit in 2017, I assume you'll want to compare 2017 (presumably with data taken after 9-20-2017) against 2015 and 2016.  The model you presented only allows the intercepts for occupancy to change over time but not the coefficients for elevation.  I would think that at minimum you'd want the intercepts and the elevation coefficients to change with year.  (Or at least having 2015 and 2016 with the same intercepts and elevation coefficients.)

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I have a follow up question for these stacked single-season models:

Should you include year in every model (as done so in the previously cited fisher and moose papers), or is it acceptable to simply include year in a subset of the models?

For my analysis (surveys from 2009-2018, points surveyed for 5 days, then resurveyed every 2-4 years depending on the point), I'm not interested in changes by year, just the associated habitat variables.

Thus, is this model set acceptable, or should year be included in each model?

m1  <- occu(data = CAT_UMF, ~ 1 ~ 1)
m2  <- occu(data = CAT_UMF, ~ 1 ~ 1 + YEAR)
m3  <- occu(data = CAT_UMF, ~ 1 ~ 1 + BDE)
m4  <- occu(data = CAT_UMF, ~ 1 ~ 1 + BPR)
m5  <- occu(data = CAT_UMF, ~ 1 ~ 1 + IMP)
m6  <- occu(data = CAT_UMF, ~ 1 ~ 1 + FPA)
m7  <- occu(data = CAT_UMF, ~ 1 ~ 1 + YEAR + BDE)
m8  <- occu(data = CAT_UMF, ~ 1 ~ 1 + YEAR + BPR)
m9  <- occu(data = CAT_UMF, ~ 1 ~ 1 + YEAR + IMP)
m10 <- occu(data = CAT_UMF, ~ 1 ~ 1 + YEAR + FPA)
m11 <- occu(data = CAT_UMF, ~ 1 ~ 1 + BDE + BPR)
m12 <- occu(data = CAT_UMF, ~ 1 ~ 1 + BDE + IMP)
m13 <- occu(data = CAT_UMF, ~ 1 ~ 1 + BDE + FPA)
m14 <- occu(data = CAT_UMF, ~ 1 ~ 1 + BPR + IMP)
m15 <- occu(data = CAT_UMF, ~ 1 ~ 1 + BPR + FPA)
m16 <- occu(data = CAT_UMF, ~ 1 ~ 1 + IMP + FPA)

Thanks!

messages.body_plain:
Hello Jim and Alex.

I came along with a solution based on Jim`s recommendation but I`m not sure that I`m doing the right thing.

I create a factor variable with three levels ( pre1, pre2, and post) indicating if the sites were sampled before ( pre1, pre2) or after the hurricane (post). In that way, I can have the intercepts and the elevation coefficients to change with year.

I needed to repeat my data 3 times in the rows populating with NA`s to get the new factor variable identifiable with my data. It seems to be working well.

Surely not the most elegant way and  I`m not sure if this can have a negative impact in model selection and other parameters estimations.

Any help is appreciated.

Thanks

Marconi

messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

please see the attached advert for an 18-month postdocin St-Andrews.

Best regads  --- Marc

-----------------------------------------------------------------------------

Vacancy for post-doctoral Ecological Statistician at Centre for Research
into Ecological and Environmental Modelling (CREEM), University of St
Andrews

Vacancy Description

School of Mathematics and Statistics, Salary: £33,199 - £36,261 per
annum, Start Date: 1 September 2019 or as soon as possible thereafter,
Fixed Term for 18 months

This is an 18-month fixed-term post. We are looking for an ecological
statistician to work as part of an inter-disciplinary project to develop
new quantitative models and analytical methods for inferring behavioural
response of marine mammal species to US Navy sonar (see Harris et al.
2018 for a recent review).  The post will involve working on two tasks
within the larger project: (1) developing algorithms for fitting
multi-species dose-response functions and applying them to experimental
data to determine which species can be grouped together in terms of
their responsiveness to sonar; (2) comparing methods for inferring
behavioural response from long-term passive acoustic data collected
during observational studies in the vicinity of Navy sonar exercises.

The first task builds upon established Bayesian methods for modelling
probability of behavioural response as a function of sonar dose (Miller
et al. 2014, Antunes et al. 2015).  These focused on single-species
analyses. Extensions have been made that allow for multi-species
modelling, including model selection for which species should share
common dose-response functions and which should be different.  However,
the current implementation is computationally expensive and hence a
bespoke algorithm, likely based on reversible jump Markov chain Monte
Carlo (RJMCMC), is desired.  Analyses of real-world experimental data
already collected is also part of this task.  The second task will
involve, at least partly, a simulation study comparing two approaches
that have already been applied to long-term passive acoustic data (e.g.,
Oswald et al. 2016): Generalized Estimating Equations (GEEs) and Hidden
Markov Models (HMMs).

We welcome applications from candidates with a PhD in Statistics or a
closely-related discipline, who have an interest in using and developing
statistical methods to solve real-world problems in ecology. Experience
with and/or research interests in Bayesian analysis, RJMCMC, HMMs and
GEEs would be highly advantageous, but is not a requirement.  The
overall project is a collaboration between ecologists, statisticians,
oceanographers and acousticians and so the ability to communicate
effectively between disciplines is essential.

The successful candidate will be based in the world-leading Centre for
Ecological and Environmental Modelling (CREEM) under the supervision of
Professor Len Thomas and Dr. Catriona Harris.  CREEM has an excellent
record of retaining research staff, so while this is a fixed-term
18-month post there may be prospects for continuation beyond that period.

For informal enquiries, we encourage those considering applying to
contact Professor Len Thomas (len.t...@st-andrews.ac.uk) and/or Dr.
Catriona Harris (catrion...@st-andrews.ac.uk).

Applications are particularly welcome from women, who are
under-represented in Science posts at the University. You can find out
more about Equality and Diversity at http://www.st-andrews.ac.uk/hr/edi/.

The University is committed to equality for all, demonstrated through
our working on diversity awards (ECU Athena SWAN/Race Charters; Carer
Positive; LGBT Charter; and Stonewall).  More details can be found at
http://www.st-andrews.ac.uk/hr/edi/diversityawards/.

Post: Research Fellow - AR2228HM

Closing Date: 5 July 2019

Please quote ref: AR2228HM

Summary info: https://tinyurl.com/y3najjvx
Further Particulars: https://tinyurl.com/yxo2yvb4

Hi all,
I'm working with unmarked for the first time and, as I have supposed, I'm occurring in a lot of errors. I have solved some of these, but I don't understand why pcount give me back an error when I choose some variables.
I have 240 sites that I have surveyed some once and some during four visits; I also have both several variables that I have recorded during each visit and some that I have recorded only one time (they describe the sites structure).
So, I have a dataset in which the sites are on rows and covariates are on columns (4 columns for repeated variables and only 1 column for site structure variables).
In order to create the model object, I'm using this script and it works

y1 <- dispar_1gen[,c(2:5)]       #surveying variable
time1 <- matrix(rep(as.character(1:4), nrow(y1)), ncol = 4, byrow = TRUE)
sc1 <- data.frame(f.erb=scale(dispar_1gen$f.erbosa), d.alb=scale(dispar_1gen$dis.alberi), hab=hab, zona=zona, row.names = dispar_1gen$Id.site)    #site variables. r, ac, af, tt
obsc1 <- list(r=r, rf=rf, ac=ac, af=af, tt=tt, hb=hb, time=time1) #observation variables

umf_1gen <- unmarkedFramePCount(y = y1,
                           siteCovs=sc1,
                           obsCovs=obsc1)

After this, I try to run the model using the following script

dm1.2 <- pcount(~ rf + hb ~ unlist(ac) + zona, data=umf_1gen, control=list(trace=TRUE, REPORT=5), mixture = c("P"))

and it give me back this error.....

Error in model.frame.default(stateformula, siteCovs, na.action = NULL) :

  variable lengths differ (found for 'zona')

If I check the object structure, I can't see anything strange

Could someone help me??? please!!!!

Michele

messages.body_plain:
Hi Marconi,

I'm not sure I completely understand the complexity of your situation, but here are a few thoughts:

I agree with making year a factor variable - yr2015, yr2016, and yr2019 would work just as well as pre1, pre2, and post (the letter at the beginning makes R recognize it as a factor variable).  With a small number of years (3 steps, basically, with a big disturbance btwn years 2 and 3), I think it's better to let the models vary freely year to year (so year must be a factor) instead of forcing a trend on the model  (which year as continuous does).

I wonder about your inclusion of a 3-way interaction with year, elevation, and transect for col and ext.  How important is transect, and should it interact with the other covariates?  What about an additive effect of transect instead?  A 3-way interaction will be very difficult to interpret, even if the models converge, no?  Plus simplifying the model complexity may help converge/identifiability issues.

Hope this helps, but I also hope those more knowledgeable than I will chime in!

-Alex

I think this is happening because you are trying to include an observation covariate (ac) with length 960 (240 x 4) in your state model, which is expecting a covariate with length equal to the number of sites (240). It also might be that calling `unlist(ac)` in the state formula is silently breaking and resulting in an empty column, which then cannot be combined with a `zona`, a  site covariate with length 240. Does the model run if you remove `unlist(ac)` from the formula? Can you summarize `ac` so that it has one value per site and put it in the siteCovs, and then change your call to

dm1.2 <- pcount(~ rf + hb ~ ac + zona, data=umf_1gen, control=list(trace=TRUE, REPORT=5), mixture = c("P"))

messages.body_plain:
Michele,

There are various potential reasons for the error messages that are hard to sort out without having all the data and code to test. However, I think they are all related to a larger issue:

If you don't have a way of summarizing `ac` so that there is a single value for each site (thus yielding a vector of length 240), then you can't include it in your siteCovs (sc1) and you also can't include it in your state formula (the second part of the formula currently `~ac + zona`. The pcount model assumes that the true abundance is constant across your repeated visits, so it doesn't make sense to try to model abundance as a function of a covariate that changes between visits, as `ac` does. You can include `ac` in the obsCovs, and the detection formula (the first part of the formula currently `~rf + hb`) because detection probability can vary between visits.

If you completely remove ac from both the siteCovs (sc1) and your state formula (so your new formula would be ~rf+hb ~ zona) does the model run?

Ken

messages.subject_clean: Time to first detection with time unit as replicate instead of site
messages.body_plain:
Previously there was discussion on time to first detection relating to ttfd over replicated sites during a single time period. We are interested in the rate of incursion of foxes into a rock wallaby colony where we know foxes are present, occupancy=1. We use N cameras around the colony to detect foxes. So I am thinking we do not need replicate sites/cameras but instead replicate time units (i.e. 12 months/units within a 1 year sampling period). We consider N cameras to be a single detector and the first detection at any camera within a time unit is a data point. The analysis remains the same but site=time unit and detection is across time units not sites.
The aim is to estimate average incursion rate over the sampling period. Does this make sense or do people think it's twaddle?

messages.body_plain:
Hi Michelle,

To get your model-averaged predictions manually, you can make your
predictions for each model separately, then use modavgCustom( ) by
supplying a vector of log-likelihoods, K, model names, predictions,
SE's. The trick with modavgCustom( ) is to make your predictions from
your data frame one row at a time.

This could be implemented in a loop or apply functions. For example,
using the example in ?occuMulti, if you wanted to model-average the
marginal occupancy of bear, you could proceed as follows:

##continuing example ?occuMulti
##assemble models in list
modList <- list("fit" = fit, "fit2" = fit2, "fit3" = fit3)

## 1) predict "bear" marginal occupancy across each model
bearFit <- predict(fit, type = "state", species = "bear")
bearFit2 <- predict(fit2, type = "state", species = "bear")
bearFit3 <- predict(fit3, type = "state", species = "bear")

##assemble in list
bearList <- list(bearFit, bearFit2, bearFit3)

##extract logL and K
logL <- sapply(modList, logLik)
K <- sapply(modList, AICc, return.K = TRUE)

## 2) iterate over each row to model average
nRows <- nrow(bear.fit)
predsModAvg <- matrix(NA, nrow = nRows, ncol = 4)
colnames(predsModAvg) <- c("pred", "se",
                           "low95", "upp95")
    for (i in 1:nRows) {

        ##extract preds and SE's
        predRows <- sapply(bearList, FUN = function(x) x[i,
                                                   "Predicted"])
        seRows <- sapply(bearList, FUN = function(x) x[i, "SE"])

        ##model-average predictions
        modAvgRows <- modavgCustom(logL = logL, K = K,
                                   modnames = names(modList),
                                   estimat = predRows,
                                   se = seRows,
                                   second.ord = FALSE)
        ##store in results matrix
        predsModAvg[i, "pred"] <- modAvgRows$Mod.avg.est
        predsModAvg[i, "se"] <- modAvgRows$Uncond.SE
        predsModAvg[i, "low95"] <- modAvgRows$Lower.CL
        predsModAvg[i, "upp95"] <- modAvgRows$Upper.CL
    }

head(predsModAvg)

Note that the predict method for fitList objects in unmarked uses the
"old" equation of the unconditional SE of Burnham and Anderson, whereas
modavgCustom( ) and other functions in AICcmodavg use the revised
equation. This explains the slight discrepancy in unconditional SE's.
See details on the uncond.se <http://uncond.se> argument in ?modavgCustom.

Hope it helps,

Marc

Dear Gwili,
 This is a tough problem and I imagine to sort it out would require that someone roll up their sleeves and take a good hard look at your data, which would be time consuming and hence no one is volunteering to do it.
 There is always a general issue of difficult likelihood estimation when you have a very large model, which you do. In these cases you can expect very unstable solutions and sensitivity to starting values, depending on whats in the model and what is not. I suspect this is your problem.
 If you have done so already , I suggest building up your model one-covariate at a time and also I recommend against using the hazard model during the build-up phase since the extra parameter is more difficult to estimate.  Finally, you might get rid of some of the habitat covariates. With so many covariates I would recommend doing a PCA on the set of them and reduce to just a few.

regards
andy

Hi Gwili,

perhaps because you have one of the 'ingredients' of those predictions, which has NaN for a standard error:

LCCode_50ForErica    -18.171      NaN      NaN       NaN

This is still a fairly complex model and so I'd not be shy to reduce complexity a little by dropping that category.

Best regards  --- Marc

Me again?!

Further to this I am confronted by another situation that I hope you might be able to shed some light on.

I have gone with a model that contains the landcovers (LCCode) as a factor with 17 levels.  I have done so because I am using the model outputs to make a spatially explicit predictive model of elephant density.  I am doing this by assigning backtransformed coefficient values to a raster of landcovers and then incorporating coefficients for the additional four continuous variables through additional rasters.  I have chosen to do this rather than predict to each site and interpolate as I am using the output to make a resistance surface for a connectivity modelling process and my study area (Mount Kenya) its very heterogeneous in terms of landcover, terrian, etc.

So, when I run my final model with all the covariates, as below, I have no problems:

> So, when I run my final model with all the covariates, as below, I have no problems:

I think there may actually be some problems with this model, as several of the landcover levels have huge standard errors. I would be hesitant to use those results.

The small number of sites for some landcovers could definitely be an issue. My approach would be to subset your data to retain only sites in the most common landcover classes (say, # of sites >30), confirm that I get a reasonable-looking model fit, and then iteratively add the remaining landcovers back until the large standard errors and/or NAs reappear. That should at least narrow down if landcover is the problem and if so which levels are causing it.

I'd also experiment with using an effects parameterization (by removing the `-1` from your formula) to see if you get better convergence with that.

Ken

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for your feedback Ken.

When using effects parameterization, the model with more detailed landcover classification (17 levels) does not output NAs, but the model with generalised landcovers (13 levels) does?!

I will try subsetting the data as you described and revert!

Cheers,

Gwili

Sent: Wednesday, 19 June 2019 14:52
To: unmarked <unma...@googlegroups.com>
Subject: Re: [unmarked] Re: Help please - unmarked distsamp models returning NAs for SE, Z and P(>|z|) values, not sure why?

> So, when I run my final model with all the covariates, as below, I have no problems:

I think there may actually be some problems with this model, as several of the landcover levels have huge standard errors. I would be hesitant to use those results.

The small number of sites for some landcovers could definitely be an issue. My approach would be to subset your data to retain only sites in the most common landcover classes (say, # of sites >30), confirm that I get a reasonable-looking model fit, and then iteratively add the remaining landcovers back until the large standard errors and/or NAs reappear. That should at least narrow down if landcover is the problem and if so which levels are causing it.

I'd also experiment with using an effects parameterization (by removing the `-1` from your formula) to see if you get better convergence with that.

Ken

messages.subject: Denominator in the chi-squared GOF test for binary data
messages.subject_clean: Denominator in the chi-squared GOF test for binary data
messages.body_plain:
I am trying to calculate a variety of residuals for goodness of fit (GOF) tests of an occupancy model in a Bayesian framework, and I can’t seem to find consensus on what should be in the denominator of the chi-squared test.

The unmarked vignette <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/unmarked/vignettes/unmarked.pdf> states, “Here we use a χ2 statistic appropriate for binary data:”

chisq <- function(fm) {

  umf <- getData(fm)

  y <- getY(umf)

  y[y>1] <- 1

  sr <- fm@sitesRemoved

  if(length(sr)>0)

    y <- y[-sr,,drop=FALSE]

  fv <- fitted(fm, na.rm=TRUE)

  y[is.na <http://is.na>(fv)] <- NA

  sum((y-fv)^2/(fv*(1-fv)), na.rm=TRUE)

  }

Here, fv = the expected (fitted) values of y (the Expectation of y, E(y)). In the last line of this function, the variance of y (Var(y)) is in the denominator; in other words, the Var(y) = fv*(1-fv), as for a Bernoulli distribution. This differs from the function suggested in the examples under the function parboot in the unmarked reference manual <https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/unmarked/unmarked.pdf> (help file):

fitstats <- function(fm) {

  observed <- getY(fm@data)

  expected <- fitted(fm)

  resids <- residuals(fm)

  sse <- sum(resids^2, na.rm=T)

  chisq <- sum((observed - expected)^2 / expected, na.rm=T)

  freeTuke <- sum((sqrt(observed) - sqrt(expected))^2, na.rm=T)

  out <- c(SSE=sse, Chisq=chisq, freemanTukey=freeTuke)

  return(out)

}

Here, the expected (fitted) values of y, E(y), make up the denominator. If applied to count data in a Poisson model, the mean = lambda = E(y) = Var(y) so it makes no difference as to which of these is in the denominator.

Inevitably, does it matter which chi-squared formulation to use? Only for a large p? For a binomial distribution, E(y) = np and Var(y) = np(1-p) and Bernoulli E(y) = p and Var(y)=p(1-p), so for a small p the variance is close to the mean E(y).

It looks like Mackenzie and Bailey 2004, including the AICcmodavg::mb.chisq() function in mb.gof.test.R <https://rdrr.io/cran/AICcmodavg/src/R/mb.gof.test.R>, use E(y) in the denominator, as do Kery and Royle 2016 in their AHMbook (p. 253). So, I’m inclined to go with that. However, the occupancy model that I specified estimates a large p.

Therefore, I’d appreciate confirmation to my lingering question (also see here <https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/1378425/relationship-between-chi-square-goodness-of-fit-testing-and-chi-square-distribut/1378523>):

Which is it? E(y) or Var(y) in the denominator of the Chi-squared GOF test for binary data (in an occupancy model)?

Thanks,

Holly

I think there may actually be some problems with this model, as several of the landcover levels have huge standard errors. I would be hesitant to use those results.

The small number of sites for some landcovers could definitely be an issue. My approach would be to subset your data to retain only sites in the most common landcover classes (say, # of sites >30), confirm that I get a reasonable-looking model fit, and then iteratively add the remaining landcovers back until the large standard errors and/or NAs reappear. That should at least narrow down if landcover is the problem and if so which levels are causing it.

I'd also experiment with using an effects parameterization (by removing the `-1` from your formula) to see if you get better convergence with that.

Ken

messages.subject: Re: density vs abund & the ranking of global models
messages.subject_clean: density vs abund & the ranking of global models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Dan,
As a novice unmarked user (and novice at modeling in general), this conversation was *slightly* hard for me to follow, so I just want to confirm what was settled on:

If I have an sample model set:
1) occu(~1~1, data=data) #null model
2) occu(~%cover+trailtype+humanactivity+month~1, data=data) #global model
3) occu(~%cover+trailtype~1, data=data) #subglobal
4) occu(~%cover+month~1, data=data) #subglobal
etc etc...

...and if model 2 (global model) was ranked as the top model with AIC( chat ~1), then I haven't learned anything, correct?

Does this mean that there is variation in my data that isn't explained by my covariates?
...I'm just having a hard time interpreting this and figuring what I need to do to fix my models so that they are meaningful!

I appreciate your help, your comments are always very useful for me!!

On Wednesday, March 11, 2015 at 9:47:35 PM UTC-4, Dan Linden wrote:
> Evan, I never presumed you didn't know what you were talking about.  That is why I made the Wayne's World comment - you are clearly an expert, there is no question.  I apologize for implying otherwise.  My intention was to focus the discussion because there are some differences with respect to the types of models fit in programs like PRESENCE and unmarked, vs. those typically fit in MARK (with some heavy overlap).  I know that you know all of this, again my comments are always with respect to unmarked users.
>
> Convenient for the sake of our discussion, we both approached my simple example from different angles.  I was not at all clear, but I envisioned the temperature covariate to be something that varied by time and space.  This is a typical situation where site is the sampling unit, as in an occupancy model.  It certainly does not apply when individual is the sampling unit, as in a mark-recapture model.  That critical detail makes all the difference here.
>
> So much of this material can be very confusing to the average user.  And it is hard to balance advocating rules of thumb vs. discouraging folks from relying on analysis recipes that sometimes lead to misguided decisions.  I guess what you hope is that people adequately familiarize themselves with the literature and seek expert opinions when possible.

messages.body_plain:
So glad to see this old thread resurrected.  :-D

To clarify, Carly, your example does not suggest you've learned nothing.  It also does not suggest unexplained variation, as far as I can tell.  A few thoughts:

1) I recommend Andy and Marc's AHM book for a very accessible treatment on occupancy in unmarked and hierarchical modeling in general: Applied Hiearchical Modeling in Ecology <https://sites.google.com/site/appliedhierarchicalmodeling/home>

2) To be clear, all covariates in your example are detection covariates.  So you haven't learned anything about variation in occupancy there.  If your objectives relate to the detection process for some species, particularly if you are designing future monitoring, and/or you have no reason to think there is spatial variation in occurrence, this could make sense.

3) I stand by my comments that having the global model rank as the top model in an occupancy analysis is not a "problem".  I am certainly open to being shown otherwise.  This thread highlights nuance that goes way beyond occupancy or the unmarked package.

messages.body_plain:
Apologies for cross postings..................experience with disease not necessary.  More important to have an ability to write and understand R code in jags, openbugs, or nimble.

We are seeking applications for a quantitative ecologist with an interest in wildlife disease. The successful applicant will assist with activities associated with the Applied Wildlife Health Research Branch and Wildlife Disease Diagnostic Laboratories Branches at the United States Geological Survey (USGS), National Wildlife Health Center (NWHC) (Madison, Wisconsin). The USGS, NWHC is a federal diagnostic and research laboratory which serves federal, state and tribal wildlife management agencies in all 50 states and US territories. Potential projects include: mark-recapture analyses, analyses of genetic data, development of models for decision making, and simulation studies. Specific duties will depend on the successful applicants interest’s and abilities.

This is a 12 month student services contract position with additional renewal for up to 2 years (pending available funding); preferred applicants will have a minimum of a M.S. (Ph.D. preferred) and either be currently enrolled in an academic program or have graduated within the past 12 months from the start date of the performance period. Start date will be September 30, 2019 or earlier. Candidates willing to relocate to Madison will receive preference.

Hours and Days: Approximately 35-40 hours/week is preferred. Candidates for part time work of at least 20 hours per week will be considered.

Desired Knowledge and Skills:

Good organizational and communication skills, including the ability to communicate with experts in other fields such as immunology, veterinary science, genetics and/or microbiology

Ability to work in a team

Minimum M.S. (Ph.D. preferred) degree in wildlife (with substantial statistical experience), statistics, or any other combination of experience and education that provides the applicant with the skills necessary to perform the duties

Ability to write clearly and concisely

Working with large data sets

Ability to code in R is crucial

Responsibilities:

Specific duties will depend on the interests and skill level of the successful appllicant. Example duties include analyses of mark-recapture data of amphibians and/or prairie dogs in relation to disease status, analyses of genetic data, conducting sensitivity analyses of simulation models, spatial-capture recapture analyses, developing decision support tools (visualization tools in R), optimization of multiple-objective decision problems, writing manuscripts, conducting basic statistical analyses such as logistic regression, sample size calculations, etc., and development of new methodology to address questions of importance in emerging diseases of wildlife.

The Student Services Contractor adheres to standard operating procedures, Good Data Management Practices and all federal safety regulations.

Required expertise/skills:

The quantitative ecologist must have a minimum of an M.S. (awarded within the past 12 months from the start date of the performance period) in a relevant field such as statistics, biology, zoology, microbiology or wildlife biology or suitable equivalent. The applicant must also be a U.S. citizen with a valid driver’s license and pass a background check. Prior research or work experience with the statistical analyses of ecological data is required. Programming skills in R are required. Candidate must demonstrate good organizational and communication (written and oral) skills for communicating with collaborators.

Desired expertise/skills:

Preferred candidate has completed a Ph.D. and should demonstrate a strong interest in statistical ecology. Previous experience with the development of R code, large data sets, manuscript writing and survival estimation, phylogenetic analyses, abundance estimation, simulation modeling, or optimizaton is advantageous.

Working Conditions:

Principal duty station – USGS NWHC, 6006 Schroeder Rd, Madison WI 53711.

messages.subject_clean: Could be this a different (and correct) way to apply multi season models?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

First, I want to thank all the experienced people who kindly provide guidelnes to new modelers, your help is priceless for all of us.

I'm analyzing a camera trap data set from years 2013, 2015 and 2017, with very sparse data (some sites were sampled only in particular years, and with varying sampling period during each year). The cameras were active many months each year (almost all year round in some cases), and the area is highly seasonal, with heavy snowfall in winter months, while dry and hot in summer (it is located in a mountain range in mediterranean ecosystem in central Chile). Some species (mainly a large ungulate) show to migrate from higher altitude sites to lower sites towards winter months, escaping from snow coverage. I used months as seasons, instead of years as normally used, for modeling relative abundance and immigration/apparent survival rates of this ungulate in the study area towards winter. I fitted open N-mixture models using monthly dynamic covariates as snow coverage or changes in NDVI. Is this approach correct? my sampling units (where cameras were located) represent the large ungulate home range observed in one month.

The years were stacked and used as covariate as I wanted to use as much data as I could. I also used 5 months of sampling from late summer days to winter months. I received some criticism and skepticism from my thesis comitee as they couldn't tell if stacking data and using months as seasons was right. I'd think it is, as I see it, only biological meaning changes, as recruitment parameter should be interpreted only as immigration, because no birth could occur during the sampling period (births only occur on spring months). I think I do not violate the assumption of closure (I account for monthly home range size of the species), and seasons have equal time interval (30 days). I should mention that I divided each month in three 10-day occasions of camera sampling, and counted total photographs of the species (independent events of 30minutes between photograph) for each 10-day occasion (that's why it should be interpreted as relative abundance).

I hope I was clear enough with the explanation and I wish someone can give his impression about this approach. What am I doing wrong?

Thanks for reading!,

José Infante.
